# Temporal Edges — When a Relationship Was True

> ⚠️ **Status: Draft — awaiting Human Operator approval** (Constitution Art. II). Phase 2 of **Edge Attributes — Facts About Relationships**, split out because it changes what an edge *is* rather than adding a field to one.
> 
> **Depends on:** phase 1 shipped, and **v28 (Opaque Node Identity)** run first — both rewrite the same tables, and its D5 rule about unattributable failures applies here too.
## 🚨 The narrowing that shapes this spec
Phase 1's draft proposed validity dates on **both** edges that cannot inherit a date from a video: `performer_tag` and `studio_parent`. Working the design through, **that was wrong for one of them.**
There are two different kinds of time, and conflating them produces a column that means different things per table:
|  | Question | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Transaction time** | When did *this library* come to believe it? | Always available — it is when the write happened |
| **Valid time** | When was it true *in the world*? | Only where a source or the operator states it |
- **`studio_parent`**** has real valid time.** An imprint is founded, acquired and retired on actual dates, and a source may know them. Modelling it records a fact.
- **`performer_tag`**** has none available.** No source supplies "blonde from 2016 to 2019". Adding `valid_from` there would create a column that could only ever be filled with a guess — and a guess stored in a date column stops looking like a guess the moment it is read back.
⭐ **Phase 1's ****`recorded_at`**** already answers everything that can honestly be known about ****`performer_tag`****'s time.** That is transaction time, it is free, and it is true.
**Therefore: this spec covers ****`studio_parent`**** only.** `performer_tag` keeps its single-row shape and gains nothing further. That collapses the blast radius from two tables to one, and from an unbounded modelling problem to a bounded one.
## What it buys — the motivating case
Not history for its own sake. **A video should resolve to the network that owned its imprint when the video was released**, not the one that owns it today.
Today a 2012 release filed under an imprint acquired in 2018 appears under the acquiring network's family, which is an anachronism the graph asserts confidently and wrongly. That is the same class of error `Impossible Data` was built to find — except this one the schema itself creates.
Secondary: a studio profile can say *"Part of ‹network› since 2015, previously ‹other›"*, which is a genuine fact about a company and currently unrepresentable.
## D1 — The shape
```javascript
-- studio_parent becomes multi-row per studio.
studio_id         TEXT NOT NULL   REFERENCES entity_profiles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
parent_studio_id  TEXT NOT NULL   REFERENCES entity_profiles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
valid_from        TEXT            -- ISO date or bare year. NULL = "as far back as we know"
valid_to          TEXT            -- NULL = still current
source            TEXT            -- from phase 1
recorded_at       DATETIME        -- from phase 1

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX studio_parent_current
    ON studio_parent(studio_id) WHERE valid_to IS NULL;
```
⭐ **The partial unique index is the whole enforcement.** *"At most one open parent per studio"* becomes a database constraint rather than an application rule, and historical rows are unconstrained. Phase 1's draft stated this rule in prose; here it is enforced by the schema, which is the only place a rule of this kind survives contact with a second writer.
⚠️ **`valid_from`**** must be nullable, so it cannot be part of the primary key.** SQLite permits NULLs in declared PRIMARY KEY columns (outside INTEGER PRIMARY KEY) and treats them as distinct — a key including it would silently admit duplicates. The partial index avoids the question entirely.
⚠️ **The existing cascade behaviour must be preserved verbatim.** The current table's comment records a deliberate choice: cascading on the parent removes the *hierarchy row*, not the child profile, so deleting a network **promotes its imprints to roots** rather than deleting them with it. A table rebuild that loses that turns a delete into data loss.
## D2 — Readers default to *now*
Four paths currently assume one row per studio:
| Reader | After |
| --- | --- |
| `parentStudioId(of:)` | current row (`valid_to IS NULL`) |
| `studioParentPairs()` | current rows only |
| `childStudioIds(of:)` | current rows only |
| `studioIdWithDescendants(_:)` | current rows only |
**Every existing caller means "now", so "now" is the default and no call site changes.** Each gains an optional `asOf:` overload rather than a new required parameter — an `asOf` that callers must pass is an `asOf` that gets passed `Date()` everywhere by people who have not thought about it.
⚠️ **`GraphSync`**** and the Studio Health audit read these too.** `danglingParents` and `parentCycles` must operate on the **current** set, or a retired parent from 2009 reports as a dangling network forever.
## D3 — Resolving as of a release date
The motivating case, stated as a rule: **the studio family view and any as-of-release lineage resolve against ****`valid_from <= release < valid_to`****.**
⚠️ **A video with no release date resolves against *****now*****.** It is the only defensible fallback — refusing to place it would drop it out of family views entirely, and guessing a date would be inventing one.
⚠️ **A row with ****`valid_from = NULL`**** matches any date at or before its ****`valid_to`****.** NULL means "as far back as we know", not "never" — and since every row migrated from today's data will have a NULL `valid_from`, reading NULL as "no match" would make every existing hierarchy vanish from as-of queries the day this ships.
## 🚨 D4 — Federation
`studio_parent` **travels between libraries**. The operator settled phase 1's attributes as local and non-travelling; validity is different, because a date is a fact about the world rather than about this library's bookkeeping.
| Case | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Receiver has the same parent, no dates; sender has dates | **Accept the dates.** Additive — filling a gap, not overruling |
| Sender has no dates (un-upgraded library) | Read as **unknown**, never as "always" |
| Both have dates and they disagree | **Reported, not resolved** — GraphSync's standing rule |
| 🚨 Both have a **different open parent** | **Refuse and report.** Inserting both would violate `studio_parent_current` and the sync would fail at the database rather than at the disagreement |
That last row is the specific hazard. Today two libraries disagreeing about a parent is a silent overwrite-nothing; once the partial index exists it becomes a constraint violation mid-merge, and the merge must detect it **before** writing rather than catching the error afterwards.
## D5 — Migration
SQLite cannot alter a primary key in place, so this is a **table rebuild**: create the new shape, copy every existing row with `valid_from = NULL` and `valid_to = NULL`, drop, rename. Every existing hierarchy therefore becomes *"current, start unknown"* — which is exactly what it is.
⚠️ **The copy must run before the partial index is created.** Today's data satisfies it by construction — one row per studio — but creating the index first would make the copy's failure mode a constraint error rather than a clean insert, and on a library that somehow holds a duplicate the migration should be diagnosable rather than cryptic.
⚠️ **Registration order, not name order.** The migrator runs in the order migrations are registered in the source, and that file is already out of numeric sequence (v23, v22, v21, v24, v26, v27, v20). Append; do not rely on the number.
## Test strategy (Constitution Art. III)
- **T1** — Every pre-migration hierarchy row survives, one per studio, as current with an unknown start. Counted, not sampled.
- **T2** — Two non-overlapping rows for one imprint both persist; the default reader returns exactly the open one.
- **T3** — Inserting a second **open** row for the same studio is refused by the database, not by application code.
- **T4** — As-of resolution: a video released before an acquisition resolves to the former network, one released after to the current one.
- **T5** — A `valid_from = NULL` row matches an as-of query for any date — the assertion that catches every migrated hierarchy disappearing.
- **T6** — A video with no release date resolves against now rather than dropping out.
- **T7** — Deleting a network still promotes its imprints to roots and deletes no profile.
- **T8** — Studio Health reports no dangling parent for a **retired** hierarchy row.
- **T9** — Federation: an upgraded library receiving from an un-upgraded one gains no invented dates; two different open parents are reported and neither is written.
## Open question for the operator
**Where would acquisition dates actually come from?** The source's studio record carries a parent but, as far as the plugin work has shown, no date for the relationship. If nothing supplies them, every row stays `valid_from = NULL` and this spec buys only the *ability* to record what the operator types by hand.
⚠️ That is a real question about whether phase 2 is worth building at all, and it is worth answering **before** approval rather than after the migration. Phase 1 is valuable regardless; this one is valuable only if the dates can be obtained.

## D4 FEDERATION — BUILT 2026-08-07
Implemented in two commits. Reading the merge changed the diagnosis twice, and both corrections are worth keeping.
### 🚨 Correction 1 — the hazard was not the one this spec named
This spec predicted a **constraint violation**: two libraries each holding a different open parent, colliding on `studio_parent_current` mid-merge. That case never arose, because the merge never got as far as a second open row. `applyGraphMerge` called `setStudioParent` for any incoming pair not already present, which for an imprint this library had placed under a different network **silently replaced the operator's answer with the sender's** — one open row throughout, no constraint to violate.
⚠️ **And it predates v30.** The old write was an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` and overwrote just as quietly. v30 made it *worse* rather than causing it: the overruled parent is now demoted into dated history, so the overrule leaves a trail indistinguishable from a real acquisition.
Now: same parent is silent, no parent here accepts the sender's, and a **different** parent is reported as a `studioParent` disagreement and written nowhere — the same treatment `tagKind` and `studioSource` already had.
### 🚨 Correction 2 — D4's first rule was unimplementable
*"Receiver has the same parent, no dates; sender has dates → accept the dates."* `GraphEdgePair` carries two ids and nothing else, so **the dates never travelled**. Every received hierarchy arrived undated regardless of what the sender knew.
`StudioParentEdge` now carries the period. The merge:
| Case | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Agreed parent, only the sender has a date | **Take it** — `datedStudioParents` |
| Agreed parent, both dated, dates differ | Reported as `studioParentDate`, neither written |
| Sender undated (un-upgraded library) | Read as **unknown** — never stamps over a date held here |
| A FORMER ownership the sender knows and this library does not | **Learned** — `newStudioParentPeriods` |
| An arriving period overlapping one held here | Reported, not written |
⭐ **Order matters, and it is asserted.** The open period is dated **first**, which stops it reaching back forever and makes room for the history behind it. Every row v30 migrated carries a nil start, so that is the common case rather than a corner one.
⚠️ Old exports decode unchanged — both dates nil, meaning *unknown*, never *always*. Newer exports decode in older builds, which ignore the two extra keys.
### 🚨 What the D4 work uncovered — the export was discarding the whole graph
Found while writing a round-trip test. `ActorLibraryExport.encode(to:)` is synthesized and has always emitted the entire graph, but `init(from:)` is **hand-written and stopped at ****`tombstones`**. So `studios`, `tags`, `performerTags` and `studioParents` were written to every `.vilmactors` file and **silently discarded on read**.
Every file-based import reported *"0 new studios, 0 new tags, 0 new connections"* while holding all of them in the file it had just parsed.
⚠️ **The live attached-library sync was never affected** — it passes the export across in memory and never round-trips through JSON. That is precisely why this survived review: the route in daily use worked, and the broken one is the between-machines route this whole federation design exists to serve.
Decoding is now tolerant, matching `tombstones`, so a file written before those fields existed still reads as *"knew nothing about studios"* rather than failing.
⭐ **The lesson worth keeping:** a hand-written `init(from:)` beside a synthesized `encode(to:)` is a standing trap — adding a property updates one side and not the other, silently, with no compiler error. Either write both or write neither.
**1,166 LibraryCore tests, 0 failures** (13 new). Both platforms build. D9 clean.
### The open question still stands
Nothing supplies acquisition dates automatically. What changed is that a date the operator types on one machine can now **reach the other**, which makes hand-entry worth doing where before it was stranded. The machinery remains correct and largely unfed.
